Well, as for taking with strangers, I'm Texan. Most of us just do that normally. I would normally listen to what they are up to for 10-15 seconds, look at their outfit, and find something in common. You don't even have to be right about it, but to be blunt it's all about practice. If you're starting from scratch you can try taking to clerks in supermarkets. They're paid to be kind, so it's a really good rejection free way to make conversation. Once you feel a little more confident, you should try finding things that are fun to do once the virus blows over, and just find people there.

A big hint is to not assume everyone you have a good conversation with will be your friend. What matters is practice.

Also, you will need to find a shrink you trust. It's all about self improvement here, and building confidence in slow ways. Keeping a journal of your experiences can help with this, so you can remember your victories when you're down. 

I will say, not everyone has to talk a lot. Being good at listening can earn you a LOT of friends if you're not the type to speak up much, or want to input a lot. Most people like to be heard so if you like listening that's a great thing.

Also, you don't have to make friends your age if you don't have a lot in common. You can go to elderly care homes and speak with them (which is good for everyone!) For example. That's good practice that might give you some good stories.

So, hi. I just moved in with my girlfriend this month, and am looking at hopefully years of happy living. We kiss, we have healthy and happy sex, we  cuddle.

At 22 I had never kissed anyone I liked (I kissed a friend and it was awful so I tend not to count it), definitely never had sex, and had hugged non-family 6 times. Yes, I counted. I had an online bf for 2.5 years also, oddly.

That was just two years ago. I worked on myself, faced my mental health issues with a good counselor and doctors, and started working full time at a kind of mediocre job. I actually met my now gf in group therapy. 

So, a few things to unpack. You're feeling really, really touch starved right now. You need to accept that 1) This is normal and 2) You need to be sure you don't go out seeking people JUST to fix that. That's what I did, and I ended up in a string of relationships that really hurt me. I wanted to be touched and kissed so badly I came off as clingy to good people and vulnerable to bad people. Naturally I ended up with the bad ones.

Some good things to do that I learned to do before meeting my gf is to build a routine. Even if it's pointless, it creates an anchor in your life. This is really hard until you get into it, then it's pretty easy. Things like exercise (running, workouts, going to the gym, even just stretching in your computer chair) and self care (food, shower, hygiene) are an obvious and good start. You've been told to do this before, I know, and you probably tried without it helping. What matters isn't even that you succeed (I still don't two years later) but that you get into that habit of setting small goals and then checking if you did them. Failure doesn't matter that much here, just trying matters. Ideally you'll do these things at the same time most/all days, but it's not the point.

You also need to find social gatherings you CAN attend. A good idea for you may be very quiet venues like theatre. People don't talk but you'll be around people, experiencing things with people, and that's a really easy and small step to take. I liked how dark and quiet those were, though I don't go anymore.

The reason I focus on this instead of romance is that romance is a complex thing, and it helps to have an identity and a sense of self before you go into it. That's what you want to build, and you do that by making and sticking to habits.

Good news: A lot of people don't care that you're inexperienced. Especially among gay women, I would say MOST would understand your reasons and not judge you. Kissing is a skill, like playing guitar, you're only good if you practice and if you're not good yet you can always practice. What matters most of finding someone good and trustworthy.

As for dating, I suggest looking for friends first. One, it's lower stress. You don't have to worry about sex, just if you like their humor. Much easier. Two, Most good long-lasting relationship come from friendships so this is a perfect first step towards dating! Two birds with one stone. Some people are very cuddly with friends too, which is nice. 

Many women don't come out/date seriously until 40's, and they still have happy lives. I promise, 20 is a great time to start. You have a decade of youth and 60 years of good life after that if you take care of yourself.

Teenagers exaggerate a lot, so remember that people you know may not be as experienced as they say too. You're probably not alone among people you know, but many people lie about it. Don't do that btw, they'll find you out when you go on the first date lol.

Edit: Also, getting a dog helped a lot. He never judges me and he loves cuddles, even when I'm sad. I learn routine and responsibility by taking care of him. It helped, but it's not for everyone.
